title: The road to Damascus (Acts 9:1–9)
hook: Saul, hunting Christians, is blinded by light and hears: why persecute me?

segments.voice: Yesterday, eunuch: the Ethiopian official Philip met on the road, and his question by the water, what hinders me?

Saul is breathing out threats and slaughter, Acts says, against the followers of Jesus, who at this point call their movement the Way. He's the young man who held the coats while Stephen died, and he's no bystander anymore. He asks the high priest for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, a week's journey north, so that any followers he finds there, men or women, can be brought back to Jerusalem in chains. He's certain, organized, on the road with his papers and companions. Just outside Damascus, at midday, a light from heaven flashes around him, and he falls to the ground.
screen: `BREATHING OUT THREATS.` → `LETTERS FOR DAMASCUS.` → `A LIGHT, AND HE FALLS.`

segments.voice: Lying in the dust, he hears a voice. In the King James Bible: "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" He asks, "Who art thou, Lord?" And the answer: "I am Jesus whom thou persecutest." Listen to that word me. Saul has never met Jesus; he's been hunting Jesus's followers. Christians have heard in that line, for two thousand years, that what's done to his people is done to him. Saul gets up, opens his eyes, and sees nothing. The men with him lead him by the hand into the city, and for three days he's blind, and doesn't eat or drink. The man who came to drag people out in chains is led in by the hand. Today's word, conversion, comes from the Latin for turning around, and the Greek word Acts uses elsewhere means the same: a turning. Two common mistakes. There's no horse: famous paintings put him on one, but the text only says he fell to the ground. And God doesn't rename him Paul here. Later, Acts says Saul, who also is called Paul: a Hebrew name and a Roman one, side by side. Paul himself, in his letters, describes this moment less as leaving his people's faith and more as a calling, the way God called the prophets. Scholars still discuss how best to describe it. Luke thought it mattered so much that Acts tells it three times, and many churches keep a feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul on January twenty-fifth. The hunter becomes the one who carries the news. The road can turn.
screen: `WHY PERSECUTEST THOU ME?` · `LED BY THE HAND, BLIND.` · `CONVERSION: A TURNING AROUND.` · `NO HORSE. NO NEW NAME.` · then, large: `THE ROAD CAN TURN.`

segments.voice: Saul only heard the voice because he was stopped. So stop, and listen to what's around you: traffic, a fridge, birds, your own breathing. Then listen inside for something you've been sure about, charging down the road with, that might need a second look. Don't argue with it. If you pray, you can ask, as Saul did, who are you, Lord?
Conversion. A turning around. Saul on the road to Damascus, stopped in the dust and led by the hand.
Your line: the road can turn. Tomorrow, someone has to go and knock on Saul's door. Day eighty.

howItsDone: Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches, among others, keep the Feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul on January 25. Many Christians speak of their own conversion as a turning, whether sudden like Paul's or slow over years.

original.note: Greek: a turning around. Acts 15:3 uses it, and the KJV renders it conversion.

what a scholar hears: Paul's own letters describe a calling like a prophet's; there's no horse and no renaming, and Acts tells the scene three times.

chat.says: Why did the voice say why persecutest thou me, when Saul had never met Jesus?
options: Christians hear that what's done to his followers is done to Jesus himself.
Saul had secretly met Jesus in Jerusalem before the crucifixion.
It was Stephen's voice, asking why Saul had stood by and let him die.
